title: Warm autumns were followed by about 7% fewer British butterflies per 1 C in 1977-2024, but the link depended on 2007 and 2012 and did not repeat in Wales, 1977-2000 or clearly in Sweden
abstract: Question: is a warm autumn (September-November) followed by fewer butterflies in the next year, as Forister et al. (2021) inferred for the western US? Data: UK Butterfly Monitoring Scheme site indices 1976-2024 (2,810 sites, 57 resident species), Swedish Butterfly Monitoring Scheme counts 2010-2024 (546 sites, 82 species) and E-OBS seasonal temperature and precipitation. Method: site x species growth models with density dependence and all other seasons controlled; year-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals; plan written before the fits. Results: in Great Britain, +1 C of autumn anomaly was followed by 7.3% lower abundance (-12.4% to -0.7%); England alone gave -7.5%. A model with year effects gave -6.8%. The link did not repeat in Wales (0.0%, -6.2% to +7.6%) or in 1977-2000 (+0.9%, -6.1% to +6.6%), and it was uncertain in Scotland (-3.1%) and Sweden (-5.3%, -11.6% to +3.9%). Without the flight years 2007 and 2012, which followed warm autumns and had very wet summers, the British estimate was -5.1% (-12.0% to +1.7%). A late-season count artefact does not explain the link: the autumn after the flight season had no link to growth (+0.7%), a skip-year model gave -6.5%, and species that do not fly in autumn had a similar slope. Species slopes were mostly negative (GB 44 of 52, none clearly positive). Summer warmth had a positive link in all samples, as in the US study. Adult hibernators, which a metabolic-cost explanation puts at most risk, had the weakest slope. If causal, British autumn warming of 0.32 C per decade gives about -0.4% per year, about one quarter of the US decline. Limitations: correlational year-to-year design, few independent years, small Welsh, Scottish and early samples, a post hoc influence check, and no test of spatial long-term trends.
